speaker: Doctor
text:
Welcome to your first visit. I see you have a newborn presenting with yellowish discoloration of the skin, which suggests jaundice. To begin, have you noticed if the yellowing started within the first 24 hours of life or is it appearing later?

Please note that since this is a newborn evaluation, I will also need to review your medical history and any available test results.

speaker: Patient
text: 5-day-old male newborn. The newborn's mother reports that her child has developed yellowish discoloration of the skin that started from the face and then spread to the trunk since the past day. There have been no changes in his bowel habits or urination. The baby was born full-term at 38 weeks’ gestation via an uncomplicated vaginal delivery and has been exclusively breastfed every 2–3 hours.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for the details. To determine the severity and cause of this jaundice, have you noticed any dark urine staining the diapers or clay-colored stools? Also, is the baby feeding well and gaining weight appropriately?

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the information; dark urine and pale stools would suggest biliary obstruction, but their absence points toward other causes. The ultrasound results should help rule out anatomical issues, and I will wait for the total bilirubin level to assess severity. Is the baby becoming increasingly lethargic or difficult to wake while feeding?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Yellowish discoloration of the skin. I also have Discoloration started from the face then spread to the trunk, Scleral icterus noted.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Physiologic Jaundice of the Newborn

Based on the onset at day 5, progression from face to trunk, exclusive breastfeeding history, and the absence of dark urine or pale stools, this is consistent with physiologic jaundice rather than biliary obstruction. The abdominal ultrasound and bilirubin levels we requested will confirm there are no underlying anatomical issues or severe hyperbilirubinemia requiring immediate intervention. Please ensure the baby continues to feed frequently to aid in bilirubin excretion.
